title: Problem Statement and Imports
content: The docstring presents Erdős Problem #1072: for a prime $p$, let $f(p)$ be the least positive $n$ with $n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$. Wilson's theorem guarantees $f(p) \leq p-1$. The two main questions ask (1) whether infinitely many primes have $f(p) = p-1$ (Wilson-maximal), and (2) whether $f(p)/p \to 0$ for almost all primes. Imports include `Nat.Factorial.Basic` (factorial definitions and basic properties), `Nat.Prime.Basic` (primality), `ZMod.Basic` (modular arithmetic), and `Filter.AtTopBot` (for limit statements).
mathContext: Wilson's theorem states $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ for every prime $p$. The function $f(p) = \min\{n \geq 1 : n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\}$ measures how early this congruence can be achieved. The sequence $f(p)$ for $p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots$ begins $1, 2, 4, 3, 8, 4, \ldots$ (OEIS A154554).

title: The Least Factorial Wilson Function
content: Defines `leastFactorialWilson p` as $\inf\{n \in \mathbb{N} : n > 0 \land p \mid n! + 1\}$, using Lean's `sInf` (infimum in a conditionally complete lattice). The set is nonempty by Wilson's theorem (which gives $n = p-1$), so the infimum is well-defined. Marked `noncomputable` since `sInf` on $\mathbb{N}$ involves classical existence. This function encodes the 'first occurrence' of the Wilson congruence before the guaranteed endpoint.
mathContext: $f(p) = \min\{n \geq 1 : p \mid n! + 1\} = \min\{n \geq 1 : n! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\}$. Well-defined since $\{n : p \mid n!+1\} \supseteq \{p-1\}$ by Wilson. The function captures how 'early' the factorial residues modulo $p$ first hit $-1$. If $p \mid n!+1$ then also $p \mid (n+p-1)!+1$ (by Fermat's little theorem structure), so the set has periodic-like behavior.

title: Wilson-Maximal Primes
content: A prime $p$ is Wilson-maximal if $f(p) = p - 1$, meaning no factorial smaller than $(p-1)!$ achieves $-1 \pmod{p}$. The term 'maximal' refers to $f(p)$ reaching its maximum possible value. Small examples: $p = 2, 3, 5$ are maximal, while $p = 7$ is the first non-maximal prime since $3! + 1 = 7$. Whether the set of Wilson-maximal primes is infinite is the first main question.
mathContext: $\text{isWilsonMaximal}(p) \iff p \text{ prime} \land f(p) = p - 1$. Equivalently, $\forall n \in \{1, \ldots, p-2\},\, p \nmid n! + 1$. This means the factorial residues $1!, 2!, \ldots, (p-2)! \pmod{p}$ never equal $-1$. Since $n! \pmod{p}$ for $n < p$ is determined by the product of residues $1 \cdot 2 \cdots n$, maximality constrains the multiplicative structure of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Wilson's Theorem and Bounds
content: Three axioms establish the basic framework. `wilson_theorem`: $(p-1)! + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for prime $p$, the classical result proved by Lagrange (1771) and attributed to Wilson (1770). `f_le_pred`: $f(p) \leq p - 1$, an immediate corollary. `f_pos`: $f(p) \geq 1$ for $p \geq 3$, since $1! + 1 = 2$ is not divisible by primes $\geq 3$. Together these bound $f(p) \in [1, p-1]$ for $p \geq 3$.
mathContext: Wilson's theorem: $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ for prime $p$. Proof sketch: the residues $1, 2, \ldots, p-1$ form the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$. Each element pairs with its inverse, except the self-inverse elements $\pm 1$. So the product is $(-1) \cdot \prod_{\text{pairs}} 1 = -1$. Consequence: $f(p) \in [1, p-1]$.

title: Question 1: Infinitely Many Wilson-Maximal Primes
content: The first main question: is the set $\{p \text{ prime} : f(p) = p-1\}$ infinite? The known maximal primes include $2, 3, 5$ but the question of whether this set is infinite is completely open. Stated using Mathlib's `Set.Infinite`, which asserts the set is not contained in any finite set. A positive answer would show that there are arbitrarily large primes where the factorial residues modulo $p$ avoid $-1$ until the very last moment.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_1072a} : \text{Set.Infinite}\{p : \mathbb{N} \mid \text{isWilsonMaximal}(p)\}$. This is a statement about the distribution of primes with a specific factorial residue property. Heuristically, for random $p$, the probability that $n! \not\equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ for all $n < p-1$ might be estimated as $\prod_{n=1}^{p-2}(1 - 1/p) \approx e^{-1}$, suggesting a positive density—but this naive model ignores correlations between factorial residues.

title: Question 2: Asymptotic Smallness of f(p)/p
content: The second main question: for 'almost all' primes (a density-1 subset), does $f(p)/p \to 0$? This would mean that typically, a factorial achieves $-1 \pmod{p}$ very early relative to $p$, not just by the Wilson endpoint. The formalization captures this via an $\epsilon$-$N$ statement: for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that $f(p)/p < \epsilon$ for all sufficiently large primes in a density-1 subset $S$.
mathContext: $\exists S \subseteq \{\text{primes}\}$ with $\text{density}(S) = 1$: $\forall \epsilon > 0,\, \exists N,\, \forall p \in S,\, p \geq N \implies f(p)/p < \epsilon$. This is a statement about the 'typical' behavior of $f(p)$: for most primes, $f(p) = o(p)$. Combined with Question 1, this would mean maximal primes ($f(p) = p-1$) are sparse but possibly infinite.

title: Hardy–Subbarao Density Conjecture
content: Hardy and Subbarao conjectured that the number of Wilson-maximal primes $p \leq x$ is $o(x/\log x)$, i.e., their density among all primes tends to zero. This is stronger than Question 2 (which only asks about $f(p)/p$, not about the proportion of maximal primes). The formalization uses $\epsilon$-$N$ quantifiers with `Finset.Icc` to count primes in an interval. If true, Wilson-maximal primes would be analogous to twin primes: potentially infinite but increasingly sparse.
mathContext: $\forall \epsilon > 0,\, \exists N,\, \forall x \geq N: |\{p \leq x : \text{isWilsonMaximal}(p)\}| \leq \epsilon \cdot x / \ln x$. Since the prime counting function $\pi(x) \sim x/\ln x$, this says the fraction of maximal primes among all primes $\leq x$ tends to $0$. The conjecture is consistent with computational evidence but no theoretical progress has been made.

title: Small Examples and First Non-Maximal Prime
content: Four axioms record computed values: $f(2) = 1$ (since $1! + 1 = 2$), $f(3) = 2$ (since $2! + 1 = 3$), $f(5) = 4$ (since $4! + 1 = 25 = 5^2$, and no smaller factorial works), and $f(7) = 3$ (since $3! + 1 = 7$). The case $p = 7$ is significant: it is the first non-maximal prime ($f(7) = 3 < 6 = 7 - 1$). The coincidence $3! + 1 = 7$ (a prime) means $7$ divides $3! + 1$ trivially. In contrast, $p = 5$ is maximal because none of $2, 3, 7$ ($= 1!+1, 2!+1, 3!+1$) are divisible by $5$.

title: Distinction from Wilson Primes
content: A Wilson prime satisfies the stronger congruence $p^2 \mid (p-1)! + 1$ (i.e., $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p^2}$). The only known Wilson primes are $5, 13, 563$, and no others have been found below $5 \times 10^{17}$. Every Wilson prime is Wilson-maximal (proved as an axiom here: if $p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1$, then certainly $p \mid (p-1)!+1$, and the question is whether any earlier factorial works). But Wilson-maximality is much weaker than being a Wilson prime—it only requires $p \mid (p-1)!+1$ with no earlier hit, not $p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1$.
mathContext: Wilson prime: $p^2 \mid (p-1)! + 1$, i.e., $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p^2}$. Known Wilson primes: $5, 13, 563$. The implication Wilson prime $\Rightarrow$ Wilson-maximal holds because if $p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1$ and $p \mid n!+1$ for some $n < p-1$, then $p \mid n!+1$ and $p \mid (p-1)!+1$, but this doesn't immediately give a contradiction—the axiom as stated requires proof that the $p^2$ divisibility somehow prevents earlier hits.
